title: My day
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The present has three singular endings: -mi for me, -si for the blunt you, -ti for he, she, and for bhavān and bhavatī. gacchāmi, gacchasi, gacchati. This course writes -mi and -ti and never -si, because -si belongs to tvam, which L2 opens — you need to know the middle one exists in order to read the other two, and that is all.

The subject is dropped whenever the ending already supplies it. gacchāmi on its own is a whole sentence, not a fragment and not poetry: the -mi has said who, and saying it twice is the only thing that would be odd.

Repeating aham in every sentence is the single clearest English accent in this language. English needs a subject because its verb barely marks one; Sanskrit's verb marks it every time, so aham is EMPHASIS — 'I, at any rate, am studying Sanskrit' — and not the ordinary way to say it.

Time words take no case and no preposition at all. adya, prātaḥ, sāyam and pratidinam just stand in the sentence, unchanged, with nothing in front of them. There is no 'in the' and nothing for the -am ending to do.

One Sanskrit present covers both English presents. paṭhāmi is 'I read' and 'I am reading' alike, and pratidinam paṭhāmi is 'I read every day'. Which one it means is the time word's business, or the situation's, never the verb's.

There is no 'am …-ing' to assemble, so there is nothing to reach for when English would build one. A learner who hunts for the word to put beside paṭhāmi usually lands on asti — and that says the reading EXISTS, which is M3's verb doing M3's job in the wrong sentence.

Here is the relief: the present marks the speaker's gender NOWHERE. gacchāmi is what a man says and what a woman says, and paṭhati is the same for both. After M1's chātraḥ / chātrā and M2's kuśalī / kuśalinī this is a rest — and M5 takes it away again.

A verb is a stem with a changeable end, and that is worth learning once: paṭhati and paṭhāmi are the same word wearing two endings, and the same stem carries the past and the future you meet next. Five verbs learned this way are five verbs, not twenty-five.
The verb is still last, and the time word is still first. prātaḥ phalam khādāmi runs time, then the thing, then the doing — and the object slot in the middle is exactly where M3 put it.

bhavān takes the very same -ti that rāmaḥ takes, and now you can see why M2 said so: 'your honour eats' and 'Rāma eats' are the same verb form, because bhavān is a third person that happens to be standing in front of you.

words.note: 'Book', a neuter noun opened in M1 — and as M3 showed, it is spelled the same acting or acted on.
The verb for reading and for studying, in the shapes this level writes: paṭhati, paṭhāmi, the past paṭhitavān / paṭhitavatī and the future paṭhiṣyāmi.

sentences.trap: There is no subject in this sentence and none is missing. English cannot leave 'I' out, so an English eye reads a gap here; the -āmi is what fills it, and it fills it completely.
sentences.sound: PUS-ta-kam PA-thaa-mi. The ṭh is retroflex — the tongue curls back to the roof of the mouth — and it carries a puff, which is what the h in the spelling is for. Before the p the m of pustakam becomes a nasal hum.

variations.changed: one ending swapped, and the person changes — with nobody named anywhere, the ending is the only thing saying who
M3's negation over a subjectless sentence; na still stands immediately in front of the verb
asked, and a subject appears only because the question has to name who is being asked

mistake.why: English builds 'I am reading' out of two words, and a learner reaching for that 'am' lands on asti. paṭhāmi is already both 'I read' and 'I am reading'; adding asti says instead that the reading exists, which is M3's verb doing M3's job in the wrong sentence.

sentences.usage: How you say what you are doing right now, and what you do generally — the same words for both.

words.note: M2's verb in its I-shape, gacchāmi. One word, and a complete sentence: the -mi ending is the subject.

sentences.trap: A single word looks too short to be a sentence, and in English it would be. Here nothing has been left out — the verb is carrying both halves of the job at once.
sentences.sound: GACH-chhaa-mi. The cch is one long held ch rather than two sounds, and the ā that follows is long — hold it. Standing alone, the word has no neighbour to join with.

variations.changed: one more word and the whole sentence is refused; na goes in front of the verb even when the verb is all there is
one ending swapped, and the sentence is about somebody else — still one word long
a time word added in front, taking no ending and needing no preposition to hold it there

mistake.why: The pronoun is not the sentence — the verb is. Drop gacchāmi and keep aham and nothing is left; drop aham and keep gacchāmi and the sentence is complete. That asymmetry is the whole of this module.

sentences.usage: The ordinary answer to 'where are you going?', and the thing you say on standing up to leave.

words.note: 'Today'. It never bends and never takes anything in front of it — a time word simply stands in the sentence.
'Sanskrit', a neuter noun opened in M1. As the thing being studied it keeps exactly the shape you already know.
The verb for reading and for studying, in the shapes this level writes: paṭhati, paṭhāmi, the past paṭhitavān / paṭhitavatī and the future paṭhiṣyāmi.

sentences.trap: English needs a preposition for most times — 'in the morning', 'on Monday'. Sanskrit needs nothing at all for these words: no preposition, no ending, no agreement with anything.
sentences.sound: AD-ya SANS-kri-tam PA-thaa-mi. The ṛ of saṃskṛtam is said ri, so the word comes out 'sanskritam'. Before the p the m of saṃskṛtam becomes a nasal hum, while adya joins nothing in front of it.

variations.changed: the time word swapped and the verb untouched — one present serves 'today' and 'every day' alike
negated, with na in front of the verb and the time word left where it was
a named subject and the he/she ending; the time word does not care whose day it is

mistake.why: adya takes no ending at all. A learner who has just met M3's -am object ending reaches for it here too, but a time word is not the thing the verb acts on — it simply stands in the sentence, unchanged, for ever.

sentences.usage: Saying what today holds, which is most of what small talk is made of.

sentences.cue: I eat a fruit in the morning.

words.note: 'In the morning'. The English needs three words and Sanskrit needs one, which takes no ending and no preposition.
'Fruit', a neuter noun opened in M1 — and neuter means the object slot cannot be seen on it.
'Eat', in the shapes this level writes: khādati, khādāmi, the past khāditavān / khāditavatī and the future khādiṣyāmi.

sentences.trap: 'In the morning' is three English words and one Sanskrit word. There is nothing in prātaḥ standing in for 'in' or 'the' — the single word is the whole of the phrase.
sentences.sound: PRAA-tah PHA-lam KHAA-daa-mi. prātaḥ ends in a visarga, a light echo of the ā before it — 'praa-ta-ha' — and before the ph it simply stays as it is. ph is a p with a puff behind it, never the f of 'phone'; kh is the same puff on a k.

variations.cue: He eats a fruit in the morning.
variations.changed: the ending moves to -ati and the sentence is about somebody else, with nobody named at all

variations.cue: I eat a fruit in the evening.
variations.changed: morning for evening — the two words swap cleanly, because neither of them takes an ending to adjust

variations.cue: What do you eat in the morning?
variations.changed: asked, with kim standing in the slot the answer will fill and the time word keeping its own place

sentences.usage: Talking about what you do at a fixed time of day — the backbone of describing a routine.

words.note: 'In the evening'. The -am on the end is part of the word and not the object ending — nothing is being acted on here.
'Write', in the shapes this level writes: likhati, likhāmi, the past likhitavān / likhitavatī and the future lekhiṣyāmi.

sentences.trap: sāyam ends in -am, which is exactly the object ending M3 taught, and it is not that ending. A time word is never the thing a verb acts on; the resemblance is an accident of spelling.
sentences.sound: SAA-yam LI-khaa-mi. The kh is a k with a puff behind it, one sound rather than two. Before the l the m of sāyam becomes a nasal hum — sāyaṃ likhāmi — while the page keeps the m.

variations.changed: the ending alone carries the change; there is still nobody named anywhere in the line

variations.cue: In the evening I write Sanskrit.
variations.changed: an object threaded in between the time word and the verb — the verb stays last, as it always does

variations.cue: Do you write in the evening? (to a woman)
variations.changed: asked of a woman, with M2's marker in front and the same third-person ending underneath

sentences.usage: Fitting an activity to a part of the day, which is how a routine gets described.

words.note: 'Every day', built from prati and dina inside one word. It bends for nothing, like every time word here.
'Water', the neuter noun M3 opened. Drinking it does not change its shape, because neuters never show the object ending.
'Drink', in the shapes this level writes: pibati, pibāmi, the past pītavān / pītavatī and the future pāsyāmi — the past drops the b.

sentences.trap: English needs a second construction for a habit — 'I drink' against 'I am drinking'. Sanskrit has one present and lets pratidinam do the rest, so there is no second form to choose.
sentences.sound: pra-ti-DI-nam JA-lam PI-baa-mi. Both m's soften to a nasal hum before the next word. The d and the t of pratidinam are dental, tongue against the teeth, and the short i of pibāmi is quick before the long ā.

variations.changed: the person carried entirely by the ending, with the habit word untouched
a different day and a refusal, both slotted in without disturbing the verb's place at the end
the same frame around a different verb — pratidinam sits in front of any of them without adjusting

sentences.usage: Habits: what you do daily, and what you are doing this minute, in one and the same form.

words.note: M2's polite you — bhavān to a man, bhavatī to a woman — and the reason the verb beside it carries the he/she ending.
Two jobs, sorted by place. Standing where the answer will stand it is 'what'; at the very front it is the yes/no marker.
'Do · make', in the shapes this level writes: karoti, karomi, the past kṛtavān / kṛtavatī and the future kariṣyāmi.

sentences.trap: English needs 'do' twice over to ask this — once as the helper and once as the verb. Sanskrit has karoti for the verb and nothing at all for the helper, because there is no helper to have.
sentences.sound: bha-VAAN kim KA-ro-ti. The m of kim becomes a hum before the k — kiṃ karoti. The r is a single quick tap of the tongue, not the English glide, and the o is long and clean.

variations.cue: What are you doing? (to a woman)
variations.changed: asked of a woman; the verb does not move, because it was third person to begin with
the I-ending, and no subject at all — kim is the only thing left standing in front of the verb
asked about somebody who is not here, on the very same ending bhavān takes

mistake.why: bhavān is closer to 'your honour' than to 'you', so the verb beside it takes the he/she ending: karoti. karoṣi is the -si ending of the blunt second person this level does not speak, and putting it next to bhavān mixes two registers in three words.

sentences.usage: The everyday opener, in person and on the phone alike.

words.note: M1's name in its acting shape. Named or not, the verb would still end -ti; the name simply says which he.
'Every day', opened just above — and it stands in the same free slot whoever the sentence is about.
The verb for reading and for studying, in the shapes this level writes: paṭhati, paṭhāmi, the past paṭhitavān / paṭhitavatī and the future paṭhiṣyāmi.

sentences.trap: English marks nothing about a man or a woman on its verb and neither does this one — but you have been trained by M1 and M2 to expect gender everywhere. Here there is none, and there will be none until M5.
sentences.sound: RAA-mah pra-ti-DI-nam PA-tha-ti. rāmaḥ before the p keeps its visarga, an echo of the ā — 'raa-ma-ha'. The m of pratidinam becomes a hum before the next p.

variations.changed: a woman, and not one letter of the verb moves — the present marks the person and never the gender
the name gone and the ending to -āmi: a whole sentence in two words
negated, with na in its one place in front of the verb and nothing else disturbed

mistake.why: -āmi is the I-ending. With rāmaḥ standing in front, the verb has to be paṭhati: a subject and an ending can never name two different people, and in Sanskrit it is the ending that gives the game away.

sentences.usage: Reporting somebody else's routine — the other half of describing your own.
sentences.mnemonic: The present sees persons, not genders.

sentences.cue: Where are you going today? (to a woman)

words.note: M2's polite you, here in its bhavatī shape for a woman — and taking the same third-person verb as ever.
'Today', opened just above. It sits between the person and the question word without bending for either.
'Where', opened in M2, standing in the slot the answer will fill — exactly as kim does when it means 'what'.
M2's verb, third person. It is the same form for bhavān, for bhavatī and for any name at all.

sentences.trap: Four words and not one of them is a preposition, a helper or an article. English would spend three of its four on exactly those; Sanskrit spends all four on meaning.
sentences.sound: bha-va-TEE AD-ya KUT-ra GACH-cha-ti. Spoken, the ī of bhavatī and the a of adya run together into a y — bhavatyadya — which is the join the page does not write. The t of kutra is dental and the r after it is a single tap.

variations.cue: Where are you going today? (to a man)
variations.changed: asked of a man — the address changes and the verb does not, because it was never second person
the address dropped, and the sentence is about somebody else entirely on the very same ending
a named person in the subject slot; the time word keeps its seat and the question word keeps its own

sentences.usage: The commonest question of the day, asked of a colleague or a guest.

words.note: 'I', M1's word. Here it is optional and therefore emphatic: the -āmi had already said it, so aham adds weight rather than sense.
'Sanskrit', a neuter noun opened in M1. As the thing being studied it keeps exactly the shape you already know.
The verb for reading and for studying, in the shapes this level writes: paṭhati, paṭhāmi, the past paṭhitavān / paṭhitavatī and the future paṭhiṣyāmi.

sentences.trap: The literal line says 'I Sanskrit I-study' and it is not a typo. The person is on the page twice, and that is exactly why an English speaker should not write it twice by default.
sentences.sound: A-ham SANS-kri-tam PA-thaa-mi. Before the s the m of aham becomes a nasal hum. Said with weight on aham this is emphasis; said flat it simply sounds like somebody who has not stopped translating.

variations.changed: aham taken away and nothing lost — which is the point of the module: it was emphasis, not grammar
negated with the emphasis kept — na goes in front of the verb, where it always goes
a time word threaded in behind the emphatic subject, still taking no ending of its own

sentences.usage: What you say when somebody else has just said what they study — the contrast is what earns the aham.
sentences.mnemonic: aham is for contrast. Otherwise let the ending speak.

comprehensionPool.cue: Today I am eating a fruit.
I study Sanskrit in the evening.
I don't go in the evening.
What are you doing today? (to a woman)
